description: We are Intellovate Red Planet Recon from Space Apps Seattle. We built Mission: Discovery, a browser game where up to four crew on their phones, or one player alone, design a CubeSat mission, launch it and find out why it worked. Every part uses real numbers from NASA's CubeSat 101, seven mini games cover launch, orbit and downlink, and a mission report gives a GO or NO GO. Play it at mission-discovery-kappa.vercel.app.
summary:
Mission: Discovery is a browser game where a crew of up to four players designs, launches and flies a small satellite mission, or one player runs all four roles alone. Players pick a mission objective, build a CubeSat part by part in a 3D clean room while live bars show mass, power, budget, data, communications and time, then play seven short mini games that cover packing the rocket, buying a launch, timing liftoff, choosing an orbit, downlinking data, trading resources and facing a design review. The game ends with a mission report: a score out of 1,000, a Concept Maturity Level, a GO or NO GO verdict from the Review Board, and the reasons behind it.

The challenge asks for a game that makes mission trade-offs concrete for students. Ours puts every trade-off in front of the player as a number they can see change, using part values drawn from NASA's CubeSat 101, and explains why a mission worked or failed instead of only saying whether it did.
details:
What It Does

Mission: Discovery turns the challenge brief's full mission loop into one sitting of play:

1. Define the Objective. Level 1, codename EMBER, is an Earth observation mission with a $1 million budget, 18 months to the launch date and a 2 year required lifetime. The crew picks one of three objectives: Spot Wildfires Early, Watch Crops and Drought, or Track Floods. Each objective lists its must-have requirements (for wildfires: see heat from fires, check Africa every day, get at least half the data home, last 2 years).

2. Design the Spacecraft. In The Clean Room, a 3D scene with the crew around the satellite, the team picks a frame (1U, 3U or 6U), solar power, battery, flight computer, optional heater and thruster, pointing system, one or two instruments, a radio and ground stations. Each part has a real mass, volume, cost and power draw, and the CubeSat in the scene changes as parts are added. Advanced parts perform better but cost more and add 2 months each to the build schedule.

3. Launch and Fly. Seven mini games, each with its own look: FAIRING (fit the parts inside the frame), LAUNCH VEHICLE (book a rideshare seat or a dedicated small launcher before seats sell out), LAUNCH WINDOW (tap when the needle is in the green), GROUND TRACK (slide altitude and tilt and watch a week of passes paint the map; lower is sharper but drag shortens the mission's life), DOWNLINK (tap to the beat while the ground station is overhead), TRADE STUDY (every role offers a part swap to close the design's biggest gap) and DESIGN REVIEW (the Review Board's questions are the design's real weaknesses, and each role answers with evidence).

4. Evaluate. The report scores the mission out of 1,000 across Science (400), Efficiency (250), Decisions (150), Collaboration (100) and Skill (100), names the Concept Maturity Level reached (CML 2 Initial Feasibility through CML 5 Concept Baseline), gives the Board's GO or NO GO, and states what worked and what hurt. Players can Fly It Again or start a New Mission, and finished runs post to a shared leaderboard.

How It Works

Two ways to play. Multiplayer: one big screen hosts the mission and up to four crew join on their phones with a room code. Each player takes a role: ZENITH, Mission Director (budget and time), FORGE, Spacecraft Engineer (mass and power), PRISM, Science Lead (data), and VECTOR, Flight Controller (communications and time). Single Player: one person plays all four roles on one screen.

One simulation for every screen. A single function takes the design and objective and returns the resource bars, every check with a plain-language explanation, and the science value, so a number never disagrees between screens.

Real physics where it matters. Power is generation against draw, with the battery sized for the 35 minutes per orbit spent in Earth's shadow. Data delivered is limited by radio rate, pass length and passes per day. Orbit lifetime, sun-synchronous timing and the 25 year debris rule are checked. GROUND TRACK uses two-body orbit motion with the standard J2 nodal drift.

Every number is sourced. Each part and rocket value carries a tag saying where it came from: NASA CubeSat 101, NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions, standard physics, a typical small-satellite value, or a value tuned for play.

No single right answer. The same objective can succeed with different frames, instruments, rockets and orbits.

Benefits and What We Hope to Achieve

Students rarely get to make a whole mission's decisions and see them collide. Here the cost of every choice is visible the moment it is made, the mini games turn abstract steps (launch windows, ground tracks, downlink passes) into something the hands learn, and the report teaches why rather than just right or wrong. It runs in any modern browser with nothing to install, so a classroom can play it on one projector and the students' own phones. Next steps: the Moon (COLDTRAP) and Mars (DUSTDEVIL) levels that the game's structure already anticipates, and more objectives per level.

Tools, Languages and Software

TypeScript, React 19 and Next.js 16; three.js with React Three Fiber, drei and postprocessing for the 3D scenes; zustand for state; Tailwind CSS. Multiplayer rooms and the leaderboard run on Cloudflare Durable Objects through PartyServer and PartySocket. Hosted on Vercel. Source code is open under the MIT license: https://github.com/intellovate-ai/mission-discovery

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. The idea, the game design decisions and every name choice are the team's (Phillip Karaya). SI (AI) was used as a tool:

Claude (Anthropic): offered design options and name sets; drafted game numbers from NASA CubeSat 101 and Design and Develop Science Missions, with each value tagged with its source; drafted on-screen text; built a font and color comparison page. The team chose every option.

Claude Code (Anthropic): wrote application code under the team's direction, including the three.js code that renders the title screen's Earth from NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble data; built the demo video, the pitch deck and the submission drafts; playtested the game and drafted the hints, the "Why This Matters" lines and the report's next step tips from the game's existing NASA sourced numbers (text only, no generated images). Commits it helped with are co-authored "Claude" in the repository history.

Higgsfield (Nano Banana Pro): generated the team logo, which carries a visible "SI generated" watermark.

Groq whisper-large-v3 and a local Whisper model: transcribed the challenge video (reference only) and timed the demo video's cuts to its narration.

Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, Chirp 3 HD (voice en-US-Chirp3-HD-Alnilam): the narration voice in the demo video is SI generated, from a script the team approved. This is stated on the video's end card, in the video file's metadata (title, comment and description tags) and in its description.

No SI-generated images or video appear in the game itself. The title screen's Earth, turning from day to night over India, is rendered by the game's own three.js code from NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble data; it is not generated imagery. The demo video shows only that shot and real gameplay captured from the live site. Every SI asset is also listed in SI-USAGE.md in the repository.
